newsitem.title: USA: US judge tosses Colo. issuer's claims vs Moody's.
newsitem.headline: US judge tosses Colo. issuer's claims vs Moody's.

text.p: A federal court judge on Tuesday refused to hear charges by Colorado's largest school district that Moody's Investors Service Inc violated U.S. antitrust laws by allegedly pressuring the locality to hire it to rate its debt.

In rejecting Jefferson County School District's antitrust claims against the rating service, U.S. District Judge William Downes ended a six-month legal battle over an unsolicited opinion issued by the rating agency in 1993 that the school district says triggered at least $769,000 in losses.

The school district originally filed a three-count lawsuit charging that the rating service committed "fraud, malice and willful and wanton misconduct" in issuing the unsolicited opinion just before the school district priced the $110 million 1993 refunding.

The school district then moved to add the two antitrust claims after the U.S. Justice Dept. last year said its antitrust division is examining "the possibility of anticompetitive practices" in the bond rating services industry."
Moody's is believed to be a key target of the probe.

Judge Downes then announced he would dismiss the first three claims filed under the First Amendment but consider the two antitrust charges. Downes on Tuesday officially dismissed all five claims, ending the lawsuit for now.

In Tuesday's 14-page opinion, Downes said, "The bond market depends in large measure upon the free and open exchange of information concerning bond issues, and the First Amendment is ultimately the best guarantor of integrity of the bond rating system."
"The court recognizes that this (ruling) works a harsh result upon plaintiff," Downes continued.

"Yet, this harm is vastly outweighed by the calamity that would result if bond rating firms could be muzzled into silence by application of the Sherman Antitrust Act to their bond rating endeavors," Downes said.
"Moody's is very pleased with the result," said Moody's attorney Robert Callagy of Satterlee Stephens Burke & Burke in New York City.
"What this reaffirms is the right of rating agencies to express opinions to the public."
